title: Post-Wedding Brunch Ideas: Planning, Menu and a Photo Reveal

faq.q: Who pays for the post-wedding brunch?
faq.a: Whoever hosts it pays. That’s often the couple or a parent, sometimes a relative or close friends, and some families split the cost. If nobody is hosting, you can still suggest a casual meetup at a café, as long as the invitation says clearly that guests order and pay for themselves, so nobody is caught off guard by the bill.

faq.q: Do you have to invite all wedding guests to the brunch?
faq.a: No, but it’s the generous default. The Emily Post Institute says the brunch usually goes to everyone invited to the wedding, and that a smaller guest list calls for discreet invitations. Many hosts limit it to family, the wedding party and out-of-town guests; if you do, invite them privately before the wedding rather than announcing it at the reception.

faq.q: What time should a post-wedding brunch start?
faq.a: Around 10 a.m. suits most weekends, with a two-hour come-and-go window so guests can leave for flights or hotel checkout without feeling rude. Start earlier if many guests fly out in the morning, or later if the after-party ran very late. Put the window, not just a start time, on the invitation.

faq.q: What should you serve at a post-wedding brunch?
faq.a: Keep it simple and filling: eggs or a breakfast casserole, potatoes or breakfast tacos, pastries, fruit and yogurt, plus plenty of water, coffee and juice. A mimosa or bloody mary bar is optional; offer a nonalcoholic option beside it. Food that sits out should follow the FDA’s two-hour rule, or one hour above 90°F.

faq.q: Do guests bring a gift to the post-wedding brunch?
faq.a: No gift is expected. The brunch is part of the wedding weekend, and the wedding gift covers the whole celebration. Guests just need to show up, eat and say goodbye. If the invitation says the brunch is no-host, the only thing guests should bring is a way to pay for their own meal.
